title: What can you say about inulin in your ads and on your site?
summary: The library supports 4 wordings for inulin; the strongest is "Supports normal bowel function by increasing how often stools are passed" (strong, 12-15 g a day). Avoid wording that names or implies a disease, a drug or a treatment, such as "Relieves or treats constipation, without 'occasional'".

supported_wordings.wording: Supports normal bowel function by increasing how often stools are passed.
supported_wordings.why: Authorized in the EU after EFSA found a cause-and-effect relationship at 12 g a day, and Health Canada lists bowel regularity uses at overlapping doses.
supported_wordings.dose_details: EU: 12 g native chicory inulin a day, and the consumer is told so. Health Canada: 10-15 g a day of chicory or Jerusalem artichoke inulin for gentle relief of constipation or irregularity, and 2-15 g a day for digestive regularity as part of a fibre-containing diet. Adults 18 and older.
supported_wordings.form: Native chicory inulin (EU); chicory or Jerusalem artichoke inulin (Health Canada)

supported_wordings.why: Health Canada lists constipation relief at these doses, and FDA's 2000 rule counts the 'occasional' form as structure-and-function wording.
supported_wordings.dose_details: Chicory or Jerusalem artichoke inulin: 10-15 g a day; agave inulin: 7.5-15 g a day. Adults 18 and older. Labeling should make clear the product is not meant for chronic constipation.
supported_wordings.form: Inulin from chicory, Jerusalem artichoke or agave

supported_wordings.wording: A prebiotic fibre that helps feed beneficial gut bacteria such as bifidobacteria.
supported_wordings.why: Health Canada lists it at 5-15 g a day, citing human studies; no other listed source covers it.
supported_wordings.form: Inulin from chicory, Jerusalem artichoke or agave

supported_wordings.wording: A source of fibre that supports a healthy digestive system.
supported_wordings.why: Health Canada lists it; no other listed source covers this wording.
supported_wordings.dose_details: Adults 18 and older. Health Canada: at least 4 g a day may be called a high source of fibre, at least 6 g a day a very high source.
supported_wordings.form: Inulin from chicory, Jerusalem artichoke or agave

wordings_to_avoid.why: FDA's 2000 rule clears only the 'occasional constipation' form.
Names a disease; no listed source supports it.

evidence_strengths.strong: At least two listed sources support it independently at a comparable dose and form, and none disagrees.
evidence_strengths.moderate: One listed source supports it as an evidence-based use at that dose, and no listed source disagrees.
evidence_strengths.limited: The only support is traditional use, the sources disagree, or the source itself calls the evidence weak.

reasons_to_avoid.drug: names a drug or presents the product as one
reasons_to_avoid.treatment: promises to treat, cure or prevent a condition

sources.name: FDA final rule on structure/function statements, 65 FR 1000 (6 January 2000), page 1015

disclaimer: Not legal advice. This guide shows the wording that published evidence supports at a daily dose, from the sources linked below; it is not a ruling on any claim. Your own product, its form and dose, and your own evidence still need to match the wording you use.
